title: Satisfaction conditions: reasonableness and good faith
shortTitle: Satisfaction conditions: reasonableness and good faith
summary: A satisfaction clause makes a party’s duty to perform depend on being satisfied with a specified performance or circumstance. The applicable standard limits how that judgment may be exercised.
notes:
Mattei distinguishes satisfaction concerning commercial quality or mechanical utility from satisfaction involving taste or judgment. The first category ordinarily calls for a reasonable-person standard; the second can require an honest, good-faith judgment. The developer’s evaluation of potential leases involved rent, tenant quality, duration, restrictions, and other interdependent considerations. Dissatisfaction with those matters differs from simply regretting the agreed purchase price. Gibson later applies the issue to a portrait. Always identify what must be satisfactory and which standard the particular decision applies.

Mattei distinguishes matters of commercial value or operative quality, commonly assessable by reasonableness, from matters of taste or judgment requiring honesty. Prospective leases required evaluation of multiple business factors, so good-faith dissatisfaction constrained the purchaser. The distinction concerns the standard governing discretion and does not make all commercial decisions objectively reviewable.
